title: Attack and defend: ARP spoofing
blurb: See how a man-in-the-middle poisons ARP caches, spot it in the logs, and stop it with Dynamic ARP Inspection.
purpose: ARP spoofing lets a device on the same VLAN quietly sit in the middle of other people's traffic. In this lab you learn how the attack works, how to spot it, and how to stop it with DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection.
scenario: On a guest VLAN (**VLAN 30**) at the branch, users report slow browsing and certificate warnings. An attacker on the same VLAN is **poisoning ARP caches** to put their laptop between the users and the gateway **10.30.0.1**. Learn how the attack works, find it, and shut it down on switch SW2. The real gateway is upstream on **GigabitEthernet1/0/1**.
topology:
Users ── SW2 ── Gi1/0/1 ── gateway 10.30.0.1
          │
   attacker laptop (Gi1/0/14)
objectives: Understand why ARP can be spoofed
Recognize the signs of ARP poisoning
Turn on DHCP snooping and DAI on the VLAN
Map the attack to MITRE ATT&CK

steps.title: How the attack works
steps.learn: **ARP has no authentication.** Any host can send a reply saying "10.30.0.1 is at my MAC", and other hosts update their caches, even if they never asked. That's ARP spoofing (or poisoning), a classic **on-path** (man-in-the-middle) attack.
steps.task: Put the stages of the attack in order.
steps.question: Order from first to last.
items: The attacker joins the same VLAN as the victims
The attacker sends unsolicited ARP replies mapping the gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC
Victims update their ARP caches and send gateway-bound traffic to the attacker
The attacker forwards the traffic on, so the victims notice little, while capturing or altering it

steps.title: Spot the poisoning
steps.question:
Which observation best points to ARP spoofing on VLAN 30?

`arp -a` on a victim:
`10.30.0.1   00-0c-29-aa-bb-cc`
`10.30.0.57  00-0c-29-aa-bb-cc`

options.text: Two different IPs, including the gateway, map to the same MAC address, and that MAC belongs to a regular user port.

options.why: A vendor prefix alone proves nothing. The giveaway is two IPs sharing one MAC.

options.text: The cache has more than one entry.

steps.title: Turn on the defense
steps.learn: **DAI** drops ARP packets on untrusted ports whose IP-to-MAC pair doesn't match the **DHCP snooping** binding table. The attacker's reply claiming 10.30.0.1 doesn't match any lease on their port, so it's dropped. The uplink to the real gateway must be trusted for both features.
steps.task: Turn on DHCP snooping globally and for **VLAN 30**, turn on ARP inspection for **VLAN 30**, and trust both on uplink **GigabitEthernet1/0/1**.
steps.hint: `ip dhcp snooping`, `ip dhcp snooping vlan 30`, `ip arp inspection vlan 30`, then `interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1`, `ip dhcp snooping trust` and `ip arp inspection trust`.

commands.explain: Builds the snooping table for VLAN 30.
Checks every ARP packet on VLAN 30 against the snooping table, which drops forged replies.
Enters the uplink toward the gateway and DHCP server.
Trusts DHCP replies on the uplink only.

commands.note: The very next spoofed reply from Gi1/0/14 was dropped and logged.

steps.title: Read the log
steps.question: SW2 logs `%SW_DAI-4-DHCP_SNOOPING_DENY: 1 Invalid ARPs (Res) on Gi1/0/14, vlan 30`. What should you do next?

options.text: Find who is connected to Gi1/0/14 and follow your incident process. The port is the source of the forged replies.
Trust Gi1/0/14 so the errors stop.
options.why: That would let the attack through again.

options.text: Turn DAI off, because it's dropping traffic.
options.why: It's dropping exactly the traffic it should.

steps.title: Name it in ATT&CK
steps.question: Which MITRE ATT&CK technique describes this attack?

options.why: Phishing is delivered by message. This attack happens on the local network.

summary: Why ARP can be forged, how two IPs on one MAC give the attack away, DHCP snooping and DAI dropping the forged replies, and the matching ATT&CK technique.
